list.listitem: Bronchiolitis is a viral illness of the lower respiratory tract in infants that causes tachypnea, bronchospasm, and mucous production. C
Diagnosis of bronchiolitis is made clinically based on the history and physical examination. B
Treatment of bronchiolitis is symptomatic. C
Bronchodilators, antibiotics, corticosteroids, and ribavirin do not improve clinical outcomes for most patients, based on the results of RCTs. B

High flow nasal canula oxygen can be used to support hospitalized patients with severe respiratory distress in the setting of bronchiolitis, but it does not prevent intensive care admission or the need to escalate respiratory support. A

Nirsevimab, a long acting monoclonal antibody, was approved by the FDA for use in the first respiratory season for all infants <8 months, unless their mother was vaccinated at least 14 days prior to delivery. It is preferred to palivizumab.A

Abrysvo is a vaccine approved by the FDA to be given to pregnant mothers for the prevention of RSV lower respiratory tract infection in infants. Abrysvo is recommended by the ACIP for all pregnant patients between 32- and 36-weeks gestation seasonally based on local RSV patterns. B

background.definition: Bronchiolitis is an illness of the lower respiratory tract in infants and young children most commonly of viral etiology. It is associated with acute inflammation and damage to the small airways with associated bronchospasm.

list.listitem: Bronchiolitis is a leading cause of hospitalization in young children.
More than 100,000 infants younger than 5 years of age are hospitalized with viral lower respiratory tract infections each year.
Of these, 75,000 are younger than 1 year of age.
The cost of hospitalization in infants younger than 1 year was more than $1.7 billion per year in 2009, the latest year for which data are available. These costs were rising from 2000 to 2009.
It is the leading cause of hospitalization in infants younger than 1 year of age.
RSV (most common cause).
Human metapneumovirus.
Parainfluenza.
Adenovirus (associated with severe disease).
Influenza.
Mycoplasma (especially in older children and adults).
Rhinovirus.
Coronavirus.
Human bocavirus.
Bordetella pertussis.
Bronchiolitis is caused by inflammation of the small airways in the lower respiratory tract, generally by viral infection.
Associated inflammation and airway edema can cause bronchospasm, V/Q mismatch, and respiratory distress.
Infection is spread by respiratory droplets/fomite spread.

Nirsevimab was recently approved by the United States FDA and recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics for use in all infants <8 months in the first RSV season, unless their mother was vaccinated at least 14 days prior to delivery. Nirsevimab is preferred over palivizumab due to lower cost and greater convenience.A

In a randomized trial of 1453 healthy preterm infants born between 29 weeks and 34 weeks, nirsevimab significantly and safely reduces the likelihood of any medically attended respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection (number needed to treat [NNT] = 14) and RSV infection requiring hospitalization (NNT = 30). A

An RCT randomized 8058 infants at 29+ weeks gestation who had no indication for palivizumab to nirsevimab or placebo. The primary outcome was hospitalization for lower respiratory infection with a positive test result for RSV, which occurred in 11 infants in the nirsevimab group and 60 in the usual care group (0.3% vs 1.5%; P < .001; NNT = 83). Severe RSV infection also occurred less often in the nirsevimab group (0.12% vs 0.47%; P = .004; NNT = 286). A

The benefit of nirsevimab was confirmed by an observational study in 15 Spanish pediatric EDs comparing outcomes before and after universal RSV prophylaxis with nirsevimab. Reductions were seen in lower respiratory infection (58%), acute bronchiolitis (59%), hospitalizations for bronchiolitis (63%) and ICU admissions (63%).A

Abrysvo is an RSV vaccine recently approved by the FDA to be given to pregnant mothers for the prevention of RSV lower respiratory tract infection in infants. Abrysvo is recommended by the ACIP for all pregnant patients between 32- and 36-weeks gestation seasonally based on local RSV patterns. B
In a cohort of 85,476 newborns, passive immunization with nirsevimab was associated with fewer RSV-related hospitalizations than maternal RSV vaccination (1.1% vs 1.4%; absolute difference 0.3%).B

Prophylaxis with palivizumab (for a maximum of 5 monthly doses during RSV season) is another option for eligible infants (). A Palivizumab prevents RSV and reduces later wheezing in preterm infants. However, it is much more expensive than nirsevimab and must be given monthly.
Hand decontamination, preferably with an alcohol-based rub, is the most important method to prevent the nosocomial spread of RSV. B

Other measures to reduce the risk of bronchiolitis include influenza vaccine according to guidelines, elimination of second-hand smoke exposure, and respiratory and contact precautions for hospitalized patients. B

A new monoclonal antibody, clesrovimab, reduced RSV-related hospitalizations in a healthy cohort of 3,614 pre-term and full-term infants compared with placebo (0.4% vs 2.3%, p<0.001, NNT=51) and reduced RSV-related medically attended visits (2.6% vs 6.5%, p<0.001, NNT=26). However, its effectiveness compared to nirsevimab has not been assessed, and it is not yet FDA approved.
Diagnosis is clinical; patients typically present with low-grade fever, cough, and wheeze. B

Physicians should assess the patient for risk factors associated with severe disease including: young age (<3 months), history of prematurity, history of immunodeficiency, history of significant cardiac or pulmonary disease, increased work of breathing, dehydration, cyanosis, and tachycardia. B
A validated clinical decision rule can also assist in the assessment of severity and need for hospitalization. A
No validated biomarker has been found to indicate disease severity or outcome. B

History of foreign body ingestion/aspiration; unilateral wheezing; afebrile early in course
No upper respiratory infection symptoms; airway sounds may be positional
Associated with a heart murmur; poor weight gain
Prolonged or recurrent wheezing; poor weight gain; recurrent respiratory infections
May have localized airway findings with predominance of crackles on examination (vs wheezing); higher fever
History of feeding difficulties; respiratory distress with feeds

list.listitem: Diagnosis of bronchiolitis is made clinically and is based primarily on history and physical examination.
Suspect bronchiolitis in infants with a history of upper respiratory tract symptoms (nasal congestion/rhinorrhea) and low-grade fever with cough and wheeze and/or crackles on physical examination.

Key features in a patient's history include age (generally infants, by definition <2 years of age), history of upper respiratory infection symptoms with worsening respiratory status, and time of year consistent with typical outbreaks. Outbreaks of RSV generally occur between the months of November to April in the Northern Hemisphere and May to September in the Southern Hemisphere. Any history of apnea should increase suspicion for bronchiolitis.

Key features on physical examination consistent with bronchiolitis include: low-grade fever, tachypnea, hypoxia, grunting, retractions, nasal flaring, wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase, and/or crackles.
Routine laboratory testing is generally not indicated to diagnose bronchiolitis.
Comorbid serious bacterial infection is uncommon in infants and children with bronchiolitis.
Nasal aspiration for RSV antigen is useful to confirm the etiology of bronchiolitis but does not change management strategies.
CXR is not useful for diagnosing bronchiolitis, and its use in lower respiratory tract infection does not reliably improve outcomes.
Pulse oximetry may be useful in predicting severity of illness by indicating the degree of hypoxemia and for monitoring hospitalized patients but is not diagnostic for bronchiolitis.
A clinical prediction rule was developed and prospectively validated to identify infants with more severe infection who may require hospitalization.

Increased severity of infection can be predicted in patients with younger age (<12 weeks), history of prematurity, history of cardiopulmonary disease, history of immunodeficiency, increased work of breathing (eg, tachypnea, grunting, flaring, retractions), dehydration, and tachycardia.
Other guidelines include evidence of cyanosis or hypoxemia in prediction rules.

A clinical decision rule was developed to identify infants with RSV who were at risk for needing intubation: lethargy, grunting, and PaCO2 ≥65 mmHg was 71% sensitive and 96% specific in predicting the need for ventilation.

More severe illness that likely requires hospital admission is predicted by oxygen saturation less than 95%, respiratory rate greater than 45 breaths/min, and age younger than 6 months. Clinical decision rules have also been developed and validated to predict the need for admission.
Supportive care, including suctioning, fluid replacement, and fever control as needed, is the mainstay of therapy for bronchiolitis. C
Oxygen should be used when necessary to maintain oxygen saturations above 90%. C

High flow nasal cannula oxygen can be used to support hospitalized patients with severe respiratory distress, but early use of high flow nasal cannula does not prevent intensive care unit admission or invasive ventilation. A
Bronchodilators (albuterol, epinephrine) should not be used in the treatment of routine bronchiolitis. B
Antibiotics, ribavirin, and corticosteroids should not be routinely used in the treatment of bronchiolitis. B
While evidence of benefit is uncertain, AAP guidelines state that nebulized hypertonic saline (3%) can be trialed for the treatment of bronchiolitis in the hospital.B
Evidence does not support the use of bronchodilators (epinephrine or albuterol) in the treatment of routine bronchiolitis.
The routine use of antibiotics, corticosteroids, antihistamines, oral decongestants, or nasal vasoconstrictors is not indicated for the treatment of bronchiolitis.

Some evidence suggests decreased mortality, respiratory deterioration, and hospitalization when ribavirin was used in patients with severe bronchiolitis or in patients with risk factors for developing severe disease. However, it is not recommended for patients with mild or moderate disease.
Evidence does not support the use of systemic or inhaled glucocorticoids for reducing hospital length of stay in bronchiolitis.
Evidence does not support the use of cool mist tent for reducing respiratory distress in bronchiolitis.

Ziresovir is an oral inhibitor of RSV F protein, which prevents the fusion of the viral particle with the cell membrane and, therefore, the infection of the cell by RSV. A trial randomized 256 infants to ziresovir or placebo. At day 3, the reduction in the bronchiolitis severity score was slightly higher in the ziresovir group than in the placebo group (3.4 vs 2.7 points; P = .002). However, an absolute difference of only 0.7 points would not meet the typical criteria for a minimal clinically important difference of at least 1.2 points.
Chest PT is not routinely recommended as it may increase the distress of ill infants without associated improvement of clinical status.
Most patients with bronchiolitis are treated as outpatients with supportive therapy alone, including adequate hydration, fever control, and suctioning using a bulb syringe or nasal aspirator.

A recent randomized controlled trial of infants with bronchiolitis discharged from the emergency department found no significant benefit of battery-operated nasal suctioning devices over bulb suctioning with respect to unscheduled healthcare revisits, parental satisfaction, infant feeding and sleeping, or parental sleeping.
Oxygen should be used as needed for patients with oxygen saturation less than 90%, and patients should be weaned when oxygen saturation exceeds 94%.

In infants with severe acute respiratory distress from bronchiolitis, heliox may reduce respiratory distress in the first hour after starting treatment (−1.15 [95% CI, −1.98 to −0.33]), but there is no decrease in rate of intubation/ventilation or length of PICU stay.

Nebulized hypertonic saline does not prevent hospitalizations or reduce length of stay in infants with moderate/severe bronchiolitis. A re-analysis of 2 meta-analyses, including 18 studies with 2063 infants, after accounting for heterogeneity, found no difference in length of stay in infants with bronchiolitis given hypertonic saline. However, 2014 AAP guidelines state that nebulized hypertonic saline (3%) can be trialed in hospitalized infants.
Duration of therapy for hospitalized patients will be based on the patient's clinical status, including hydration, level of respiratory distress, and oxygen saturation.

Discharge may be considered for patients who are able to maintain adequate oxygen saturations, in whom respiratory rate and effort normalize, who are able to take fluids by mouth, who are hemodynamically stable, and who are able to be cared for at home.
Hospitalization should be considered in patients with persistent hypoxia (O2 saturation <90%), respiratory distress, apnea, lethargy, or failure to take fluids by mouth.

It should also be considered in infants with comorbid conditions that would impair cardiopulmonary status (hemodynamically significant congenital heart or lung disease) or with acidosis or who are unable to be cared for at home.
Intubation and mechanical ventilation may be required for respiratory failure, persistent hypoxia, or apnea.

Intravenous hydration is used to maintain adequate hydration in patients unable to take fluids by mouth or who have significant respiratory distress that raises the likelihood of aspiration of fluids.

Once a patient is hospitalized, respiratory status must be closely monitored using serial clinical examinations. A randomized controlled clinical trial of 229 infants greater than 4 months of age suggests that outcomes are similar in hospitalized children with stable bronchiolitis who are monitored with intermittent versus continuous pulse oximetry.
Hydration status should also be followed clinically.
Respiratory and contact isolation are recommended for hospitalized patients.
Infection is generally self-limited, but wheezing after an episode of bronchiolitis may last for 2 weeks to 1 month or more depending on initial severity of illness. C
Bronchiolitis is generally self-limited.
Most patients are asymptomatic after about 2 weeks, although respiratory symptoms (including wheeze) may persist for over 1 month in those most severely affected.
Recurrent infection is common; however, subsequent infections tend to be less severe.
Infants hospitalized with bronchiolitis may have a higher incidence of respiratory problems, including bronchospastic disease, as they get older.

A clinical prediction rule was developed and prospectively validated to identify infants with more severe infection who may require hospitalization. Patients with younger age, increased work of breathing (eg, tachypnea, grunting, flaring, retractions), dehydration, tachycardia, cyanosis, and hypoxemia have more severe infection.
Case fatality ratios for infants with bronchiolitis range from 0% to 1.7% for RSV and 0% to 0.17% for all-cause bronchiolitis.
Follow-up should be recommended for patients who exhibit difficulty breathing, persistent wheeze, or decreased oral intake/fewer wet diapers.

For patients who are managed in the outpatient setting, caregivers should be told to seek medical attention for the following: evidence of respiratory distress (tachypnea, retractions, grunting, flaring), apnea, lethargy, cyanosis, high fevers, and failure to take adequate hydration.

Parents should be taught nasal suctioning with saline drops and a bulb syringe or nasal aspirator before feeds. Other supportive measures include fever control and assurance of adequate oral hydration.
If hospitalization is necessary, close contact with the patient's primary care physician is important to ensure follow-up after discharge.

cell.label: History, physical, and respiratory assessment. Toxic or in severe respiratory distress?
Suction, assess respiratory status, and start O2 if SaO2 is consistently 91% or less. Medication trial desired?
Single-dose trial with epinephrine or albuterol. If improved, consider repeated inhalations.
Manage without medications (nasal suctioning, oxygen, monitoring).
Period of observation. Ready for discharge (RR <70, room air, oral feedings, family can provide care and monitoring, follow-up scheduled)?
Discharge home with parent education and primary care physician follow-up.
Monitor until ready for discharge, or admit. If admitted, consider cardiopulmonary monitoring, frequent respiratory and SaO2 checks, and suction before feeding and as needed.

feature.feature_body: Infants born at less than 29 weeks gestational age during the first year of life. Infants with chronic lung diseas Infants with chronic lung diseas of prematurity (preterm infant born at less than 32 weeks gestation who required >21% oxygen for at least the first 28 days of life) during the first year of life.Infants with CLD chronic lung diseasof Infants with hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease in the first year of life. Otherwise healthy infants with gestational age 29 weeks or greater should not receive palivizumab. Data from Ralston SL, Lieberthal AS, Meissner HC, et al.; American Academy of Pediatrics. Clinical practice guideline: the diagnosis, management, and prevention of bronchiolitis. Pediatrics 2014;134:e1474–e1502.
